verses.verse:
सरी गमौ पधौ निश्चेत्येते सप्तस्वरा मताः।
एकैकस्मात् समारभ्य मूर्छनाऽभ्यस्यते बुधैः।८८।
verses.text: Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha and Ni: these are held to be the seven notes. Beginning from each one in turn, mūrchanā is practised by the wise.

commentary.text: Although we have seated the seven notes on these holes in order so that it is easy to understand, it is not necessary that the hole we have given the place of 'Ma' should always be 'Ma'. If we take the second hole as 'Sa', the third hole can be 'Re'. In ancient times this procedure was called mūrchanā. It would not be inappropriate if we called it the svara sāriṇi procedure. In the making section of this book I have placed all the notes taking ('Ma') as 'Sa', which is the common practice. Here, for the first practice, the first hole is taken as 'Sa', which later on will be taken as 'Pa'. Then again, now and then, for one's own convenience, any one of the above 7 notes may be taken as 'Sa'.
See the svara sāriṇi figure below —

The practitioner should practise 5 of these mūrchanās a hundred times each. And sometimes practise taking all 16 notes up from bottom to top and down from top to bottom in one breath. But do not forget to increase the force of the breath step by step, and then to reduce it on the way back. In this practice keep the speed only such that no note is lost or skipped over and left out. The speed of the fingers will naturally increase little by little, and the breath too will become long. Only when at least two ārohāvaroha (ascents and descents) in one breath are mastered should you consider yourself qualified to play the bānsurī.
